Phosem · Client contract, in progress SW · AI · ML · CNN

Phosem — PIN Diode Defect Classification

I built a CNN + MIL pipeline from scratch that doesn't just flag pass/fail on microscope images of PIN diodes — it identifies why a die failed inspection in the first place.

Client :Phosem (PIN diode manufacturer) Role :Defect detection with PatchCore & classification (team of 2) Stack :PyTorch · PatchCore · MIL · CNN
0.0%
Selective accuracy at 89.7% coverage
0.000
Average precision (2.56× the baseline)
0.000
F1 score for junction-defect detection
What I Learned
  • The challengeIn an early experiment, defect-detection recall came out at a ‘perfect’ 1.000. Checking the confusion matrix showed the model was simply flagging every die as defective. The cause was a threshold bias from training on a 9:1 good-to-bad ratio.
    The fixInstead of reporting that number as-is, I used it as the reason to redesign how labeling and thresholds were set.
  • The challengeThere were no pixel-level labels, only pass/fail labels for the whole die. Since defects cover only 1–3% of a die's area, copying the die label onto every patch meant patches with no defect at all were still labeled ‘bad,’ and training was quietly falling apart.
    The fixI brought in Multiple Instance Learning: labels are assigned at the level of an 8-patch bag, and loss is computed only from the highest-scoring patch in that bag.
  • The challengeMicrometer-scale particles were getting erased whenever the full image was resized.
    The fixI switched to 128×128 sliding-window patches at 50% stride. At inference time, 144 overlapping patches are collected per die, so no defect ever falls entirely outside a window.
  • The challengeClient and mentor feedback needed to translate into real performance gains, not guesswork.
    The fixI ran three formal improvement cycles — ROI-restricted sampling, threshold calibration, test-time augmentation, and seed ensembling — validating each one with a quantitative before/after comparison before folding it in.
  • The challengeIt wasn't clear whether breakage defects were even detectable as a signal in optical images to begin with.
    The fixI checked with a HOG + logistic regression control experiment. Junction defects separated cleanly from good dies (AUC 0.90); breakage didn't (AUC 0.43–0.60) — evidence there was no signal in the image at all. Rather than chase a metric the data couldn't support, I proposed dropping breakage from the image-AI scope entirely.
  • The challengeIt wasn't clear whether the remaining errors were a limit of the model, or a problem with the data and labels.
    The fixA second, independent HOG + logistic regression control experiment showed the remaining errors weren't a model-capacity limit — they came from ambiguous ground-truth labels right at the decision boundary.
Building conv and FC layers by hand on top of a CNN, and working through MIL training, taught me CNN-based image AI from the inside — and let me build a full pipeline start to finish on my own.
→ github.com/ilfpns/PhoSem
NCRC · NAVER Connect Robotics Cup 2026, Preliminaries AI · RL · Robotics

NCRC — Tuning a Humanoid Walking Policy's Reward Inside a Locked Codebase

Competition rules allowed exactly one thing to be touched — nine reward weights in a single dictionary. So I turned tuning into a method instead of a guess: comparing against the official reference, running low-cost probe experiments, and finally a full 12,000-iteration training run.

Competition :NAVER Connect Robotics Cup 2026 (Preliminaries) Role :Solo reward tuning (the only part of the codebase I was allowed to touch) Stack :IsaacLab / IsaacSim · RSL-RL (PPO) · H1 Humanoid
9
Reward weights — the only values in the entire codebase I could change
92.4%→20.0%
Fall rate, from default to final submission
7.33
Best reward — 2.5× the first 12,000-iteration candidate (2.96)
What I Learned
  • The challengeh1_task/, train.py, and play.py were all off-limits. The only thing I was allowed to touch anywhere in the competition codebase was a nine-value REWARD_WEIGHTS dictionary.
    The fixI worked inside that strict constraint, producing every performance gain through reward design alone.
  • The challengeRunning the first training pass with default values, the robot would just stand there and then tip over sideways. The fall rate hit 92.4%.
    The fixI traced it to a termination penalty that was far too weak, and fixed that one value first (-5 → -100) instead of changing several at once.
  • The challengeThe robot could stand, but the policy was shaky, and ang_vel_xy_l2, joint_deviation_hip, flat_orientation_l2, and feet_air_time were all tangled up in it.
    The fixRather than change them all at once and lose the causal signal, I adjusted them one at a time and isolated the factor that actually fixed the side-to-side instability.
  • The challengeThe first 12,000-iteration candidate plateaued. Reward stayed stuck at 2.96, with heading drift and exploration std both stubbornly high.
    The fixInstead of tuning by feel, I compared against IsaacLab's official H1/G1 reward configuration. Both action_rate_l2 and track_ang_vel_z_exp were sitting at roughly half the reference values — that gap was exactly what was holding performance back.
  • The challengeFeeding a fix straight into a 12,000-iteration training run risked wasting a huge amount of time if the direction turned out to be wrong.
    The fixI ran the two suspect values through a cheap 3,000-iteration probe first. Once I confirmed reward and heading tracking improved without hurting the fall rate, I reran the full 12,000-iteration training from scratch. Every metric improved over the first candidate (reward 2.96→7.33, fall rate 23.0%→20.0%, heading error roughly 1.2→0.70).
  • The challengeI couldn't be sure the files I submitted actually matched what had been trained.
    The fixI hashed the final policy.pt and env.yaml with SHA256 and cross-checked them against the actual training run's output and several timestamped backups, verifying the uploaded files matched the trained result byte for byte.
What actually broke the plateau wasn't more trial and error — it was comparing against IsaacLab's official H1/G1 reward setup. Two of the nine values were each sitting at half the reference level.
Fire-Gas · JumpUp 2026, Nonamed Club Project AI · Firmware · LLM

Fire-Gas — LLM-Generated Training Data for an Edge Fire Classifier

With no real sensor dataset to work from, I used an LLM directly as part of the data pipeline — and before trusting its output, I caught it myself generating data that made no physical sense.

Program :JumpUp 2026 (Nonamed club project) Role :Owned the full pipeline: data → model → real-time inference Stack :ESP32-S3 · LSTM · LLM-based data generation
50,000
Rows of synthetic training data generated by prompting an LLM with real-world examples
14
Features — 9 raw gas/environment channels plus 4 derived ratio features
0.00
Correlation between MQ5 gas and CO in the initial dummy dataset — the number that exposed the physics was wrong
What I Learned
  • The challengeThere was no real sensor data, so I couldn't get a training dataset at all.
    The fixI built a pipeline that generates training data directly by prompting an LLM (Codex) with real per-channel examples, expanding the dataset across the BME/MICS/SCD/MQ5 sensor channels from 10,000 rows to 50,000.
  • The challengeThe correlation matrix on the initial dummy dataset showed a 0.00 correlation between flammable-gas readings and CO. Real combustion chemistry (flammable gas → incomplete combustion → CO) should show a clear correlation. The data simply didn't make physical sense.
    The fixBefore trusting the model, I caught the error in the tool itself. I concluded that generating physically consistent synthetic data means encoding the causal relationship before asking for statistically plausible numbers, and redesigned the generation process around that.
  • The challengeThe nine raw channels alone weren't enough for the LSTM to pick up the subtle signal changes of a real fire scenario.
    The fixI handled missing values with linear interpolation and added four derived features (gas_composite, voc_ratio, co_co2_ratio, heat_humidity), feeding all 14 features into an LSTM that reclassifies every 15 seconds.
  • The challengeClassification accuracy hit 100% after a single epoch, and severity MAE dropped to 0.02 — a symptom of training data that was too simple and never grounded in real measurements.
    The fixInstead of presenting that as a win, I treated it as a red flag first — and identified where the model actually struggled: the 15-second inference cycle couldn't keep up with fast changes, producing spikes whenever severity shifted abruptly.
  • The challengeThe device wasn't hitting its target real-time response speed. The cause was an unnecessary vTaskDelay, unrelated to the AI computation itself, blocking the inference loop.
    The fixI defined a target response time first, measured against it, and stripped out the blocking I/O down to the bare minimum inference actually needed.
The most common bottleneck on this project was never the model — it was a meaningless Delay() call. Define your target response time before you start stripping anything out.
→ github.com/Fire-Gas
WIFY · PIUDA National Competition, 2026 Firmware · IoT · AI

WIFY — Camera-Free Fall Detection for Care Facilities

It detects falls in care-facility bathrooms using nothing but WiFi signal distortion — no camera, so no privacy risk — and I built the entire communication stack myself, from the device up to the cloud.

Program :PIUDA (NIPA × Japan, a Korea–Japan elder care product competition) Role :Firmware & communications (team of 3) Stack :ESP32 · BLE GATT · MQTT · WiFi CSI
7
Care facilities I cold-called myself for field validation
≤20B
Fixed-length BLE payload — fits the default MTU with no negotiation needed
1
Race condition eliminated by redesigning the flow instead of adding a lock
What I Learned
  • The challengeThere was no standard for the ESP32 fall-detection device and the Android app to communicate reliably, and BLE's default 20-byte MTU made text formats like JSON inefficient.
    The fixI wrote a versioned BLE GATT protocol spec (v1.0) and implemented both ends myself: a fixed-length little-endian binary payload, a custom 128-bit UUID namespace, and a sequence-numbered notify channel designed to stay reliable even over a lossy wireless link.
  • The challengeI needed a consistent way for the device and server to exchange telemetry, remote WiFi reconfiguration, and baseline recalibration commands.
    The fixI designed the MQTT topic hierarchy and pub/sub flow myself and implemented it on both the ESP32 firmware and the server.
  • The challengeTwo FreeRTOS tasks were reading and writing a shared ‘baseline ready’ flag at the same time, and it was causing a real race condition.
    The fixInstead of adding a mutex, I fixed it by restructuring the flow itself so the two tasks never touch the same state at the same time in the first place.
  • The challengeI had no way to know whether a camera-free fall detector would actually hold up in a real care facility.
    The fixI cold-called seven care facilities myself and did an in-depth interview with a staff member at one of them. Their answer — “residents respond better to sound and light alerts than phone push notifications” — led me to rework the UX direction.
Sensing had to work without a camera, and the protocol had to hold up in a real facility's WiFi environment, not just a lab. Both constraints came from picking up the phone and calling care facilities before I wrote a line of firmware.
→ github.com/Wave-based-Intelligent-Fall-Identifier
WRO · WRO Korea 2026, National Final CV · Robotics · Firmware

WRO — Vision Pipeline for an Autonomous Robot

A color-block detection and steering pipeline for a Raspberry Pi robot navigating a course whose obstacles get rearranged on competition day — open-sourced, with a tuning tool I built myself so my teammate could reuse it.

Competition :World Robot Olympiad, National Final Role :Camera & AI (team of 2) Stack :OpenCV · Raspberry Pi · Python
2
Public repos, complete with handoff documentation
4.7×10.5cm
Block dimensions — the reference value for parameters that hold steady across any course
0
Shape-based parameters that never need retuning between courses (only exposure and color get readjusted)
What I Learned
  • The challengeSetting thresholds by feel for color-based block detection kept producing false positives and misses.
    The fixI implemented HSV-based color and block detection alongside geometric blob filtering, and tuned it with a calibration tool I built myself.
  • The challengeStarting the tuning process by trying to detect blocks first kept loosening the color values until I had to start over from scratch.
    The fixI deliberately fixed the tuning order: start from an empty course and narrow in toward true positives, never the other way around. Loosening a threshold from the false-positive side doesn't break one edge case — it breaks the whole model.
  • The challengeObstacle placement changes on competition day itself, but there was never time to rebuild the pipeline from scratch each time.
    The fixI documented which parameters change with the course (exposure, saturation/brightness thresholds — readjusted every competition) versus which stay fixed by the block's physical dimensions (aspect ratio, extent). As a result, a new course means a few minutes of retuning, not a rebuild.
  • The challengeEven when a teammate took over, it was hard for them to keep developing with the same context I had.
    The fixI organized the handoff into two public repos plus a CLAUDE.md, so a teammate's AI coding tool wouldn't start from zero — it could pick up the exact same project context I'd been working with.
Once you separate what changes with the course from what stays fixed, a new environment stops meaning a rebuild — it just means a few minutes of retuning.
→ github.com/DSM-Nonamed-WRO/tune → github.com/DSM-Nonamed-WRO/WRO-Rasp-EM-Code
ABC · Paid Work Experience Program AI · Frontend · Product

ABC — Multimodal AI Platform for Field Work

A field inspector types “find the potholes in this photo,” and the platform returns automatically detected, segmented, and labeled training data. I owned the interface that makes it usable without ever knowing what a VLM is.

Team :4 people, a corporate-partnered program Role :Frontend + AI-assisted rapid prototyping Stack :LLM · VLM + SAM · Hybrid RAG · Agents
4
People on the team in this corporate-partnered program
4
AI components unified behind one UI (LLM · VLM+SAM · Hybrid RAG · Agents)
1
Raspberry Pi server I built and ran myself to host the deployed prototype
What I Learned
  • The challengeA multi-model backend built from an LLM, a VLM, SAM auto-labeling, hybrid RAG, and agents was simply not something a non-technical field worker could operate directly.
    The fixI designed a UI/UX layer that turns all of it — including the hybrid RAG spanning internal data and public data portals, and the agent that recommends the next task — into a flow a non-technical user can actually run.
  • The challengeWaiting for a finished spec before building the frontend meant our pace was locked to when the backend happened to be done.
    The fixI used AI-assisted (“vibe coding”) prototyping to move quickly from requirements to a working UI, iterating on the interface alongside the backend team instead of waiting for a finished spec.
  • The challengeThe deployed prototype needed an actual server to demo and run on.
    The fixI built and operated the team's Raspberry Pi server myself.
This is the other half of the spectrum Phosem shows: the same person training a CNN from raw pixels on one project, and building a product on top of a foundation model on another.
→ github.com/DSM-Pixel
